title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking

target_networks.name: ReLU policy network (1 x 16, Frozen Lake)
ReLU policy network (2 x 32, Transporter / Stock Market)

domain: safe sequential decision-making / formal verification (probabilistic model checking)

headline_result.text: LLM-written ReLU policies reached the Storm-computed optimal probability in all 18 runs (2 LLMs x 3 environments x 3 seeds) already after the creation step, and satisfied a PCTL until safety requirement in all 6 runs.
headline_result.quote: With two LLMs on three environments, the created policy of each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability, before any dataset or model-checking feedback.

evidence_quality.held_out_eval: partial: three-job transporter was never shown to the LLM

key_claims.claim: Every returned policy is verified exactly by the Storm model checker rather than estimated by simulation.
key_claims.quote: The model checker Storm computes, rather than estimates from simulations, the probability that the policy satisfies the requirement, so every returned policy is verified.

key_claims.claim: Four of six two-job transporter policies also complete three jobs with probability 1; the other two complete them with probability 0.
key_claims.quote: Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task that the LLM never saw.

key_claims.claim: In one run dataset repair raised accuracy to 98.4% but broke the safety requirement; one model-checking round restored it.
key_claims.quote: In one of them, dataset repair raised the accuracy to 98.4% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.

key_claims.claim: Dataset accuracy is only a proxy: networks with 39% accuracy still reached the optimal probability.
key_claims.quote: Both networks show that accuracy is only a proxy: with 39% accuracy, they still reach the optimal probability

key_claims.claim: The most common generation error is a wrong matrix shape (48% of DeepSeek answers, 29% of Kimi answers), suggesting the LLM loses count on long matrices.
key_claims.quote: The most common error is a wrong network shape, in 32 of the 67 answers of DeepSeek-V4-Pro (48%) and in 8 of the 28 answers of Kimi-K3.1-Pro (29%).

limitations_stated.text: Only three runs per configuration and non-deterministic cloud inference, so numbers are indicative.
limitations_stated.quote: Each configuration runs three times, and cloud inference is not deterministic even at temperature 0, so our numbers are indicative rather than precise estimates

limitations_stated.text: Environments and networks are small (at most 16,496 states, two hidden layers of 32).
limitations_stated.quote: The environments and networks are small (at most 16,496 states and two hidden layers with 32 neurons)

limitations_stated.text: PRISM models and Frozen Lake are public, so contamination cannot be ruled out.
limitations_stated.quote: so we cannot rule out that the LLMs saw these models or related policies during

notes_for_review: Adds formal verification (PRISM/Storm via COOL-MC) as the judge for LLM-written policy weights, which is a stronger check than game score. The tasks are small symbolic MDPs where the LLM effectively hand-compiles a rule policy into ReLU step functions, so success shows rule-to-weight translation more than learning; there is no RL-trained or random/null baseline. The repair loop was needed in only 1 of 24 runs, so its value is barely tested; code is released on GitHub.
